skeletons.name: two_identical_images
skeletons.why: the FIRST image is lifted and the second stays literal — so the two languages must agree on which one is the reference AND on the bytes of the one they left behind

skeletons.name: sidecar_distinct_images
skeletons.why: the sealed_local shape: two DIFFERENT images, so a language that lifted the wrong one produces a different ref AND a different skeleton, which the same-image case above cannot distinguish

skeletons.name: sidecar_engine_swapped
skeletons.why: same document, different engine digest — pinned by a RELATION to sidecar_distinct_images, since 'the engine is part of the measured artifact' is otherwise asserted only by the staleness diff

skeletons.name: sidecar_reordered
skeletons.why: the engine listed first: the lifted ref becomes the ENGINE's (which no node release list contains) and the structure moves with it

skeletons.name: sidecar_substituted_image
skeletons.why: refused: a `${VAR}` second image is pinned by nothing — dstack hashes this document BEFORE expansion, so one skeleton digest would cover every engine the operator later supplies

    network_mode: "service:kronk"
  kronk:
    image: ${ENGINE_IMAGE}
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"

skeletons.name: engine_config
skeletons.why: the THIRD lifted span: the engine's own config, so two operators on different hardware can size it differently and still match one release

skeletons.why: a `content:` at the sentinel's OWN indent is a sibling entry, not that entry's body, so it must not be lifted — the depth test is strictly deeper, and a `<` there measured a document TS and Go disagreed about

skeletons.name: engine_config_sentinel_carries_a_value

skeletons.name: sidecar_wrong_algorithm
skeletons.why: refused: sha512 is not the algorithm the rule names, and a well-formed digest of the wrong kind is the shape a lenient prefix check waves through

skeletons.name: sidecar_interpolated_repository
skeletons.why: refused: the digest half is literal, so this DOES content-address the bytes — it is refused because the rule is spelled `<repository>@sha256:<hex>` and no registry accepts `${` in a repository name. Pins that `${VAR}` is rejected wherever it appears, not only when it covers the whole reference.
